title: Naan-e barbari
subtitle: Persian flatbread with sesame and nigella seeds
excerpt: Naan-e barbari is a thick, oval Persian flatbread with a glossy, golden crust and a soft, chewy crumb inside. It is brushed with a cooked flour and water glaze called roomal before baking, which gives it its characteristic sheen and the ridged surface that catches seeds.
sourceNotes: Najmieh Batmanglij, Food of Life: Ancient Persian and Modern Iranian Cooking and Ceremonies (1986). Naan-e barbari described as the most widely eaten Iranian bread, baked in specialist bakeries every morning. Margaret Shaida, The Legendary Cuisine of Persia (1992). The roomal glaze technique and the ridging method documented.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze baked and cooled flatbreads. Reheat in a hot oven for five minutes.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The dough can rise overnight in the fridge. Shape and bake from cold, adding five minutes to the baking time.
recipe.temperatureNote: Fan 210 degrees / gas 8. Preheat for at least 20 minutes.

content.text: Naan-e barbari is the most common Persian bread: thick, oval, and slightly puffy with a deeply golden, shiny surface from a cooked flour glaze called roomal. The roomal is a quick paste of flour and water cooked briefly on the hob, then brushed over the shaped dough before baking. It caramelises in the hot oven and gives the bread its distinctive glossy crust. Sesame and nigella seeds are scattered on top and press into the ridges.
Mix {{yeast-dried}} and {{caster-sugar}} into 320 ml of warm water. Leave for five minutes until foamy.

Combine {{strong-bread-flour}} and {{sea-salt-fine}} in a large bowl. Add the yeast liquid and {{olive-oil}}. Mix to a rough dough and knead for ten minutes until smooth and elastic. The dough should be soft but not sticky.
Cover and leave in a warm place for 60 to 90 minutes until doubled in size.

Whisk {{plain-flour}} with 100 ml of cold water in a small saucepan until smooth. Cook over a medium heat, stirring constantly, for two to three minutes until the mixture thickens to a thin paste. Remove from the heat and cool slightly.

Preheat the oven to 230 degrees and line two large baking trays with baking paper. Divide the dough into two pieces. On a lightly floured surface, stretch each piece into an oval about 35 cm long and 15 cm wide. Lay on the baking trays.

Brush the roomal glaze generously over the top of each bread. Using your fingers, press five or six lengthways grooves along the surface, pressing firmly but not cutting through. Scatter {{sesame-seeds}} and {{nigella-seeds}} into the grooves.
Bake for 15 to 18 minutes until deeply golden and the base sounds hollow when tapped. Eat warm.

items.symptom: The crust is pale and not glossy
items.cause: Roomal glaze not cooked to the right consistency, or not enough applied
items.fix: Cook the glaze until it is noticeably thick and paste-like. Apply it generously and evenly right to the edges.
The dough must double in size during the prove. In a cool kitchen this can take two hours. Do not rush it.
Rest the divided dough for ten minutes before stretching. This relaxes the gluten and makes it easier to shape.

items.symptom: The seeds fall off after baking
items.cause: Seeds scattered on rather than pressed into the glaze
items.fix: Press the seeds lightly into the surface after scattering. The grooves hold them during baking.

content.text: Naan-e barbari is the most eaten bread in Iran, baked fresh every morning at noonvayi (breadshops) that open before dawn. Customers queue to buy it hot, and it is eaten at breakfast with white cheese, butter, honey, or jam, or as the bread alongside the main meal. It is identified by its long oval shape, the ridged surface, and the glossy sheen from the roomal glaze: a flatbread without these features is not barbari. The name refers to the Barbari people, Hazara from Afghanistan, who historically sold this style of bread in the Tehran bazaars.
